PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the text as it is normally printed the Inspector’s outer
garment is not a running stage property, it is a barometer. 

In the Constance Garnett / usual English text Ochumelov is introduced
as “a little, plump man in a new overcoat” and the new overcoat is
then kept before the reader at every change of colour in the
chameleon. 

* 1.  He arrives in the new overcoat / new uniform, the outward sign
of his little official self-importance;
* 2.  he is at once made anxious for the cleanliness of the garment
when the crowd and the mud of the pavement threaten it – the coat is
the thing he does not want to get dirty;
* 3.  the coat is again made conspicuous as he fusses with it,
brushes it, takes care of it and finally makes a show of it when the
possibility of General Zhigalov’s ownership appears, i.e. the moment
at which fear makes him servile.

That is three distinct symbolic sketches of the garment, the word
‘overcoat/coat’ being made to occur four times in the Garnett text,
each occurrence marking one of Ochumelov’s fear-driven changes of
attitude to the dog and to the crowd. It is the tripartite – in the
literal count four-mention – sketch that is normally quoted as the
coat’s symbolic shorthand for his shifting, servile mentality.

detailed physical description at all, it is only used as a stage-property and the
references to it are the markers of Ochumelov’s change of colour.

times and the two put-on / take-off moments are the ones that are normally
read as the symbolic shifts.

* He comes out to the crowd in his overcoat.
* In the middle of the scene, when he is momentarily feeling his authority
secure, he takes his overcoat off and then puts it on again.
* He leaves the scene still in the overcoat.

three references to the garment – essentially the two shifts of mentality, a
take-off and a put-on-back-on, with an initial reference to him being in it.
It is the two changes of dress that are read as the chameleonic change of
mood; the third mention is the conventional opening/closing reference to the
overcoat.  Most commentators therefore speak of three mentions / two
symbolic changes of the coat, the two put-on/take-off moments being the
paradigmatic ones.
